newsitem.title: PERU: Peru rebels free hostage as tense siege continues.
newsitem.headline: Peru rebels free hostage as tense siege continues.

text.p: Marxist rebels holding hostages in the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima freed a sick police commander early on Sunday, but his release did little to ease tensions in the 40-day standoff.
Gen. Jose Rivas Rodriguez, a deputy chief in the Peruvian national police, was wheeled out of the compound on a hospital trolley flanked by Red Cross officials and Bishop Juan Luis Cipriani.
Lying face up with his bare feet sticking out from under a blanket, Rodriguez was taken to an ambulance and driven to a nearby police hospital.
International Committee of the Red Cross representative Michel Minnig said the rebels agreed to free Rodriguez on medical grounds. He did not say what was wrong with him.
But there was little prospect of an early release for the remaining 72 captives held by the heavily-armed Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels.
Shortly after dawn on Sunday the MRTA made the now daily broadcast of its rebel hymn from inside the residence and shouted that they would hold out until their demands were met.
"We've been here for 40 days and we are going to continue resisting," an unidentified rebel yelled over a megaphone.

Rodriguez was the first hostage to be freed since Jan. 17. His release followed a day of tense posturing, with rebels firing warning shots into the air in response to what they called provocative movements by the police outside.

Armoured vehicles have moved near the residence twice, a police helicopter has flown over the compound, and troops armed with high-powered weapons and night-vision equipment have rushed to the perimeter wall, their rifles pointed at the building.

The Red Cross, which has expressed public concern about the recent police activity, said the two shots fired on Saturday caused no injuries. "We ask for calm so as not to put any lives at risk," Red Cross representative Ruben Ortega said.

In an apparent effort to calm nerves, the government vowed to seek a peaceful end to the crisis. "We are going to take the time needed to reach a peaceful solution to this crisis without bloodshed," Prime Minister Alberto Pandolfi said.
But he gave no clue to how the government hoped to end the standoff, which has stalled over its refusal to consider the MRTA's main demand for the release of 400 jailed comrades.

President Alberto Fujimori, whose younger brother Pedro remains among the captives, also sought to defuse tension, insisting that recent police manoeuvres were routine and not the precursor of an assault.
"What we need is a period with not much talking but time for everyone to reflect," he told a news conference after a two-hour meeting with government negotiator, Domingo Palermo.

While firmly rejecting rebel demands to set their comrades free, Fujimori has offered the roughly 15 hostage-takers safe passage to another country if they lay down their weapons and release all the hostages.

Palermo said he had held a preliminary meeting with a commission of "guarantors" who will oversee eventual talks. "The Red Cross is preparing for the MRTA to eventually come out for the start of conversations," he said. "I am going to be very clear. There is no deadlock."
About 100 Japanese tourists arrived at the siege site early on Sunday with messages of peace and conciliation for the hostages and their captors.

The tourists, members of the non-governmental "Peace Boat" organisation that arrived in Lima on Friday, carried banners in the shape of hearts and said they hoped to deliver hundreds of origami sculptures to the hostages.
The rebels took more than 500 hostages on Dec. 17 upon storming a cocktail party at the diplomatic mansion, but have freed most of them in what they called "goodwill gestures."

The remaining captives in the mined and booby-trapped residence include two Peruvian ministers, congressmen, judges, police and army chiefs, the Japanese and Bolivian ambassadors and about two dozen Japanese diplomats and businessmen.
Red Cross officials have repeatedly said the remaining hostages' health was stable despite claims from individual family members and colleagues that some were sick.
